name: Laryngoplasty / Adam's apple surgery

lead: Chondrolaryngoplasty, popularly called a tracheal shave, trims the thyroid cartilage to flatten a prominent Adam's apple and smooth the front of the neck. It is among the more common surgeries for transgender women and is also sought by others who want a less prominent Adam's apple.

A surgeon makes a small incision and shaves the cartilage, sometimes endoscopically through the chin or mouth. The result is directly visible, and Wikipedia reports most patients are satisfied, with complaints mostly about residual prominence or scarring. It was first described in 1975.

paras: It is done by a surgeon as a short procedure, with about two weeks of recovery. The voice is usually unaffected.

The vocal folds sit close to the cartilage, so rare damage and slight pitch changes are reported. Swelling, bruising and temporary swallowing difficulty are common during recovery, and scarring is possible.

angle.text: Chondrolaryngoplasty shaves the thyroid cartilage so the Adam's apple looks flatter and the neck front smoother, often sought for a more feminine contour. The change is visible right away, and published series report mostly satisfied patients.

lead: Chondrolaryngoplasty, popularly called a tracheal shave, reduces the thyroid cartilage that forms the Adam's apple, the bump at the front of the neck. People have it done to flatten the neck profile so the throat looks smoother and, for many, more feminine. The nickname is a misnomer because the trachea is not involved.[1] Wikipedia describes the goal as a throat that appears smoother and less angular.[1]

The Adam's apple is the laryngeal prominence, the angle of the thyroid cartilage around the larynx. It is usually much more noticeable in adult men, where cartilage growth and forward movement during puberty, driven mainly by testosterone, make it stand out; in women it sits higher and is often small.[2] Chondrolaryngoplasty is among the more common procedures for transgender women and is also sought by others who want a less prominent Adam's apple for aesthetic reasons.[1][3]

The operation was first described by Francis G. Wolfort and Richard G. Parry in 1975. The voice is usually unaffected, though slight pitch changes have been reported, and most patients are satisfied.[1] Surgical reviews describe it as commonly done as part of facial feminization surgery and emphasise preserving laryngeal integrity while reducing the prominence.[3][4]
infobox: Tracheal shave, chondrolaryngoplasty, thyroid cartilage reduction

paras: The Adam's apple is formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage in front of the larynx, and it protects the front of the larynx and the vocal cords behind it.[2] In typical adult male anatomy the larynx is larger and sits further forward, so the bump is more visible, while in women the prominence sits on the upper edge of the cartilage and the smaller larynx makes it much less noticeable; many women nonetheless have a slight visible protrusion, which is not normally considered a medical disorder.[2] The growth at puberty is driven mainly by rising testosterone, and the same larger larynx contributes to a deeper voice.[2]

For appearance, the neck is the lower end of the face-and-neck profile, and a prominent laryngeal bump is one of the more visible sex-linked cues there. Surgeons describe chondrolaryngoplasty as making the throat look smoother and less angular, and people who want a more feminine neck contour, or simply a less prominent bump, use it to change that single feature.[1][3] Because the change is limited to cartilage, it leaves facial hard and soft tissue unchanged, which is why it is often combined with other procedures in one facial feminization operation.[3][5]
The English name is a calque of the Latin pomum Adami, which appears in European medical texts from about 1600, and the formal anatomical term prominentia laryngea dates to 1895.[2]

In the standard approach a surgeon makes a small horizontal incision, often in a skin fold at the base of the Adam's apple, and shaves the cartilage with a scalpel under local or general anesthesia. Newer variants place the incision under the chin or inside the mouth and may be done endoscopically.[1]

Surgical reviews describe visualising the vocal cords with flexible laryngoscopy and using intraoperative needle localisation of the anterior commissure to guide how much cartilage is removed, which is intended to protect voice outcomes.[3][4] The procedure can be combined with other facial feminization surgeries.[3]

Wikipedia says the surgery is usually outpatient unless combined with other procedures, with local or general anaesthesia depending on whether it is the only operation. The muscles are held apart, the cartilage is shaved with a scalpel, and the incision is closed with sutures, usually placed in a skin fold to limit scarring.[1]

A review of the technique describes the aim as maximally reducing the thyroid cartilage prominence while preserving laryngeal integrity and minimising external scarring, and reports that the bronchoscopic-assisted approach with intraoperative needle localisation has reliably produced safe and effective results with a low risk of complications.[4]

Swelling, bruising and difficulty swallowing or speaking are common to varying degrees. The red incision line lasts about six weeks and full recovery averages about two weeks; many surgeons recommend rubbing the incision to limit visible scarring.[1]

Because the vocal folds lie close to the site, they can rarely be damaged, and slight pitch changes have been reported.[1] Most patients are satisfied; the usual complaints are that the Adam's apple still looks too large or that the scar is noticeable.[1] Wikipedia notes feminization laryngoplasty, a more complex procedure that also alters the vocal cords, can address insufficient reduction but changes the voice and carries more risk.[1][2]

Wikipedia notes that removing too much cartilage can weaken the airway and cause breathing difficulty, which is why reviews emphasise localising the anterior commissure and visualising the vocal cords.[1][3][4] Some patients add vocal surgery at the same time to reduce voice-related dysphoria.[1] Recovery may take longer when conditions such as anaemia are present.[1]

Surgeons who publish on the technique emphasise that the amount removed is limited by laryngeal anatomy: taking too much cartilage risks weakening the airway and affecting the voice, which is why feminization laryngoplasty, a more extensive operation, is reserved for cases where a shave is judged insufficient.[1][2]

sections.h: Use in facial feminization and cosmetic care
paras: Chondrolaryngoplasty is described as most commonly performed as part of facial feminization surgery for transgender patients with a diagnosis of gender dysphoria.[4] Wikipedia's article on facial feminization surgery places Adam's apple reduction in the lower-face group of procedures, alongside chin reduction, jaw reshaping and masseter reduction, and notes that hormones can soften facial fat distribution but cannot change bone or cartilage structure.[5]

Facial feminization surgery grew out of maxillofacial, otolaryngology and plastic reconstructive surgery; surgeon Douglas Ousterhout is credited with pioneering many procedures after a 1982 request.[5] Insurance coverage varies by country, being described as common in France, Belgium and the Netherlands and expanding in the US under the Affordable Care Act.[5] Anyone wishing to reduce thyroid notch prominence for aesthetic reasons may consider the operation.[3]

A different group of operations changes the voice rather than the cartilage shape. Pitch-reduction thyroplasty is described in a review as being used mainly in transgender men who do not get enough pitch reduction from speech therapy and masculinising hormone therapy.[6] Some transgender men also seek to enlarge the prominence, and testosterone can enlarge the larynx.[2]

Feminization laryngoplasty, an alternative, can further reduce the Adam's apple after a shave and retighten the vocal folds, with additional risks and effects on the voice.[1] Laryngeal framework surgery and office-based laryngology are covered in separate reviews.[7][8]

No randomised trials of chondrolaryngoplasty were found. The evidence consists of surgical technique reviews of the procedure,[3][4] and the literature cited by Wikipedia, which includes a 2019 systematic review of esthetic reduction of the thyroid cartilage in JPRAS Open, a 2018 patient-satisfaction study by Cohen and colleagues, and a 2008 report by Spiegel and Rodriguez of surgery under general anaesthesia with a laryngeal mask airway.[1] Those sources report most patients as satisfied.[1] Studies of facial feminization surgery as a whole conclude it can improve well-being and quality of life by reducing gender dysphoria, with a low complication rate.[5]

A distinct group of trials examines injection laryngoplasty for vocal fold paralysis and glottic insufficiency, such as cross-linked hyaluronan versus collagen with two-year follow-up; these concern voice and not the cartilage-shaving operation.[9]
